It's more about psychology than anything else. I had problems (and still occasionally have) with a specific type of nerve pain. Every time it starts acting up, I go on some sort of cleansing diet. Now, I KNOW it doesn't matter - food generally doesn't make my nerve better or worse (it is not triggered by any allergies, etc.). On the intellectual level, I know that I just have to wait it through.

But, on the emotional level, I start to panic. I hate this pain; it is horrible, and I am scared. To regain some sort of illusion of control, I change my diet - not dramatically, but enough to feel I have some impact on something I have limited to zero impact on. Then I feel I have some measure of control over my body, and I feel healthier, less - how to put it? - 'polluted' by this pain.

I wish more healthcare professionals understood the mental mechanisms behind this. You don't need to explain this to me - I KNOW these things don't work. But when doctors cannot help me, I would use any rituals and tricks to convince myself I am actually DOING something.

It's like with placebo and alternative remedies - of course, they don't work, but they fulfill an important psychological role. You cannot take it away from people and give them nothing instead.

I am glad you wrote about your experiences.

When you have an ongoing problem, you will do literally ANYTHING, no matter how silly it sounds. At the height of my nerve pain, if someone told me to chant at a crossroads at night - I would run and do it. It's hard to blame people for trying whatever they can, even if it sounds silly (although, of course, if it psychologically helps them, it is not that silly).

I think the problem arises when people start taking homeopathic pills instead of proper medicine. And you are right - people in pain (and scared) are vulnerable and easy to exploit. There are many individuals who are eager to take advantage of that and take their money (sometimes by scaring them further).

It is very scary when someone refuses conventional treatment in favor of drinking herbal teas, but if someone is undergoing a treatment and, at the same time, seeks alternative therapies - why not? Very often what these treatments provide is, above all, some sort of meaning and narrative to people's suffering. It is not enough for many people to know they have a serious illness - they need a meaning, they need to know WHY they have it, in a more philosophical sense. And if they find something that helps and does not interfere with other treatments, why not?

It's a tough decision - I'm sure some of these issues are authentic - but it truly is challenging to identify the real ones amidst the sea of disorganized recollections and so on. Kudos to you for attempting to sort them out.
